Preface To 1918 Supplement
This volume is a compilation of allthe laws of a general and permanent
nature enacted by the General Assembly at itsregularsessionsin1916 and 1918,
and at the specialassembly convened by the Governor on February 14, 1917,
and endingApril25, 1917, which latterwas calledto consider"the subjectof
revenue and taxation." The new legislation, which includesalllaws enacted
since the publicationof the last (1915) editionof the Kentucky Statutes, has
been given itspermanent Kentucky Statutes sectionnumbers .
In addition there have been included, as annotationsto the new as well as
to the old sectionsof the Kentucky Statutes,notesfrom the decisionsof the Court
of Appeals rendered since the editionof 1915 down to about the adjournment
for the summer recess of 1918 .
Not only have allthe new laws been compiled but an endeavor has been made
by the editorto indicatethe statusof theretoforeexistinglaws as affectedby
the new legislation, the old law as amended being insertedin full. A valuable
featureof this1918 Supplement willbe found to be the historicalreferencegiven
in italicsin parentheses followingeach section, thus indicatingthe laws from
which each particularsectionhas been drawn . The great value of thisreference
willbe immediately appreciatedby the practitionerand by the court wherever
the historyof the legislationis involved in the constructionof the statute. The
present editioncarriesthe legislationback to the sessionof the General Assembly
of 1891, the firstto follow the adoption of the present Constitution.
As the titleof every Act is a vitaland essentialpart of every statutethe
editor believesthat this volume has been made more nearly complete by the
insertionof a Table of Titles of the severalActs compiled, in order that the
person having occasion to referto the Kentucky Statutes to ascertainthe law
may be enabled to find the complete law in one book . The titlemay govern
both the question of validityand the constructionof the law . It would seem ,
also, that a copy of the titlesof Acts in a place convenient for referencewould
induce more frequent consultationof the titlesof the laws and , therefore, more
accurate understanding of the effectof the legislation. Thus ,from thehistory
of the legislationgiven aftereach sectionthe user may refer,by the number of
the chapterof thesessionactstheregiven,directlyto the titleof that chapter as
given in the Table of Titles. Conversely, anyone having the chapter or page
number of a particularlaw in the sessionacts may , by referenceto the Table
of Titles,findat a glancewhere that law ispermanently compiled in the Kentucky
Statutes. An Act relatingto some purely localcondition,e. g., repealingthe
specialcharter act of some town or school, or an appropriationact not per-
manent in itsnature,as not providing a continuingannual appropriation,isnot
deemed of a general and permanent nature and has been marked "not com-
piled" in the Table .
Great care has been observed in editing the laws contained in this 1918
Supplement to the Kentucky Statutes,and it is hoped that, by its practical
use, the bench and bar and others having occasion to referto the lateststatute
law will commend the inclusion of the several new features mentioned .
THE BALDWIN LAW BOOK COMPANY
Incorporated
LOUISVILLE , KENTUCKY .

classification.title: An Act to provide an electric system of workmen's compensation for industrial accidents, prescribing the manner of election and the rights and liabilities of employers, employes and third parties; making provision for medical and surgical care of injured employes; establishing rates of compensation for personal injuries or death; providing methods of insuring and securing the payment of such compensation; making minors sui juris for certain purposes; creating a board to administer this Act, prescribing the duties, powers and rights thereof and imposing a tax upon insurance premiums, also a tax upon employers who carry their own risk for the maintenance of such board and providing a system of appeal to the courts from the decisions of such board; prescribing certain penalties, with an emergency clause, and appropriating certain sums to meet the expenses of putting this Act into effect, and repealing all laws and parts of laws in conflict therewith, to the extent of such conflict.
classification.summary: This act establishes a system for workmen's compensation for industrial accidents. It outlines the rights and liabilities of employers and employees, provides for medical and surgical care, sets compensation rates for injuries or death, and details methods for insurance and securing payments. It also makes minors sui juris for specific purposes, creates a board to administer the act, imposes taxes on insurance premiums and self-insured employers for the board's maintenance, and establishes an appeal process to the courts. Penalties are prescribed, and an emergency clause is included. The act repeals conflicting laws.

The confidence is high as the subject matter is clearly industrial safety and compensation, not racial segregation or discrimination.

The confidence is high due to the explicit naming of the institution which was a common characteristic of segregated education.

classification.title: An Act to repeal an Act entitled, "An Act to incorporate and establish a public school for colored people in the town of Hawesville , and within a radius of two miles of the court house in said town ," approved March 19 , 1888, and all amendments thereto.
classification.summary: This act repeals a previous act that incorporated and established a public school specifically for colored people in Hawesville. This repeal suggests a potential shift in how educational facilities for Black children were managed or funded, and its inclusion in a list of statutes from 1918, a period of active Jim Crow legislation, warrants its classification as such.
classification.reasoning: The statute explicitly mentions 'colored people' in relation to a public school. While it is a repeal of a prior act, the act being repealed established a separate educational institution for Black children. The repeal itself, in the context of Jim Crow era legislation, could indicate a consolidation or alteration of segregated educational structures. Therefore, it is classified as Jim Crow with an explicit racial indicator and a category of education.

This directly points to racial segregation in housing. Although the U.S. Supreme Court reversed the specific ordinance, the fact that it was a subject of constitutional discussion within Kentucky law during this period indicates its relevance to Jim Crow practices. The mention of 'equal, though not necessarily identical, privileges' also aligns with the discriminatory logic of Jim Crow laws, where 'equality' was often interpreted as separate but unequal.

classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes, along with its annotations, discusses the constitutional requirement that laws must relate to a single subject, which must be expressed in the title. The core principle is that the title of an act must accurately reflect its content to avoid unconstitutionality.

classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky Constitution, as interpreted by court cases in 1918, deals with tax rates and indebtedness. It clarifies what constitutes indebtedness for the purpose of constitutional limits, discusses the validity of debt contracted for current expenses, and outlines the process for exceeding tax levies for specific purposes like sinking funds or road improvements. It also specifies that the tax rate limitations do not apply to school purposes and that assessments for draining districts are not considered taxes under this section. The section also touches upon the requirement for a two-thirds majority vote to incur indebtedness contemplated by section 158.

The content focuses on fiscal matters, specifically tax rates and municipal/county indebtedness. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly discriminate based on race. The interpretations discuss the application of tax limits to various governmental functions and the procedures for incurring debt. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

The surrounding text discusses how this section, along with others, was affected by later legislation aiming to create a uniform system for dog licensing and protection of livestock.

The text focuses on property damage and personal injury caused by dogs, with specific exceptions related to the location and time of the incident (owner's premises, day/night). There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly target or discriminate against any racial group. The context of the discussion is the regulation of dogs and the protection of livestock, not racial segregation or discrimination. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

title to the Act of May 1, 1893 , с. 190 , p . 842 , Section 26 of which was compiled as

It would not seem open to serious doubt that the provisions of the Act of 1893

done by it, may reasonably be held to have been included in the title. Assuming that
the same provisionsof the Act of 1906 forming Section 68a-5 could fairlybe held to

cerning mad dogs - be taken as repealed because not included in this " complete sys-
tem ?" Because of the uncertainty on this point Section 68a-5 has not been omitted
from this compilation preceding a decisionon the question.

repealedby thissectionwould remain unaffectedby this Section 68a-5. As Section 68

classification.summary: This statute outlines regulations for railroad, telephone, and telegraph companies regarding the publication and filing of their rates, fares, tolls, and charges. It mandates that companies must publish schedules of their rates in legible form and keep copies available for public inspection at their depots and stations. Changes to these rates require at least thirty days' notice to the public and the Railroad Commission, with proposed changes published in new schedules. The Railroad Commission has the discretion to allow changes with less notice or modify posting and filing requirements under certain circumstances. It is unlawful for companies to charge rates different from those published in their schedules.

classification.summary: This statute, divided into sections 209 and 210, addresses the legal concepts of champerty and maintenance. Section 209 discusses contracts that aid in the prosecution or defense of suits, referencing a court opinion that a stranger to a contract cannot attack its validity on grounds of champerty. Section 210 deals with the sale of land adversely held and actions to subject such land. It clarifies that possession rendering a conveyance champertous must be actual and to a well-defined boundary. It also states that a conveyance of land by a woman in possession to a third person, when the grantee was already in possession, was champertous and void, and did not suspend the statute of limitations in her favor. classification.title: CHARITABLE AND CORRECTIONAL INSTITUTIONS
classification.summary: This statute outlines regulations for charitable and correctional institutions, specifically concerning the licensing, examination, and revocation of licenses for institutions caring for the feeble-minded, epileptic, or insane. It details procedures for transferring individuals between state institutions and private licensed facilities, and mandates health officers to initiate proceedings for the segregation and custody of feeble-minded persons likely to reproduce. It also prohibits poor houses from housing feeble-minded females under forty-five if space is available in specialized institutions, and makes it unlawful to aid the marriage of feeble-minded persons. Finally, it allows for the admission of mentally defective persons to state institutions for the feeble-minded and epileptic under special agreements for compensation, provided there is room.

It also allocates an additional $75.00 per year per pauper idiot for the erection of additional dormitories and buildings, to be paid to the board of control. The statute also states that the present allowance to pauper idiots will cease when the new provisions take effect.
classification.reasoning: The statute discusses appropriations for a farm colony for the 'feeble-minded' and mentions 'pauper idiots'. While the term 'pauper idiot' could potentially have been used in a discriminatory manner historically, the statute itself does not contain any explicit or implicit racial classifications or segregation. It focuses on the care and housing of individuals deemed feeble-minded or pauper idiots, regardless of race. Therefore, it is not classified as a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: Kentucky School for the Deaf - Colored Pupils Per Capita Allowance
classification.summary: This statute amends a previous act to ensure that the per capita allowance for pupils in the school for the colored deaf is the same as that provided for pupils in the school for the white deaf. It also addresses compulsory education for deaf children.
classification.reasoning: The statute explicitly mentions 'school for the colored deaf' and 'school for the white deaf', indicating a racially segregated educational system. The provision for equal per capita allowance between these segregated schools, while seemingly equitable on the surface, is a direct consequence and perpetuation of Jim Crow segregation in education. Therefore, it is classified as a Jim Crow law. The document type is 'codes' as it refers to sections of 'Kentucky Statutes, Carroll's Edition, 1915' and is presented as part of a codified set of laws. The confidence is high due to the explicit mention of racial categories in the context of separate institutions.

classification.title: Kentucky Statutes, Section 6810-6: Beneficiaries and Financial Accounts of Children's Benefits
classification.summary: This statute outlines the regulations for benefit contributions and financial accounts related to children's benefits within a society. It specifies that these funds must be kept separate and distinct from other society funds, and details conditions under which benefit certificates can be surrendered and exchanged. It also addresses the continuation of certificates if the primary supporter's membership terminates and defines eligible beneficiaries for death benefits, including spouses, blood relatives up to the fourth degree, in-laws, step-relatives, legally adopted step-children, and dependents. It also allows for members to become dependent on charitable institutions and have their benefits transferred with consent.
classification.reasoning: The statute discusses the financial management of benefit contributions for children and the eligibility of beneficiaries for death benefits within a society. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly create racial distinctions or segregation. The statute appears to be purely administrative and financial in nature, related to insurance or fraternal organizations. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: Fraternal Congress Table of Mortality and Investments for Fraternal Benefit Societies
classification.summary: This statute outlines the requirements for fraternal benefit societies regarding mortality tables, disability benefits, deferred payments, investments, and the distribution of funds. It specifies that societies must use mortality tables adopted by the National Fraternal Congress or higher standards, with interest assumptions not exceeding four percent. Investments must be in securities permitted for life insurance companies in Kentucky, or in accordance with the laws of the society's state of incorporation if it's a foreign society. Funds collected for mortuary or disability purposes cannot be used for expenses. The statute also details the process for organizing a fraternal benefit society, including the minimum number of incorporators, the content of articles of incorporation, and the election of officers.
classification.reasoning: The statute pertains to the regulation of fraternal benefit societies, focusing on financial solvency, investment practices, and organizational procedures. It does not contain any language or provisions that suggest racial discrimination or segregation. The requirements are applied generally to all such societies operating in Kentucky. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: An Act to Amend Section 762a of the Kentucky Statutes Relating to Fire Insurance Rates
classification.summary: This statute outlines the powers and duties of a board in regulating fire insurance rates. It grants the board the authority to investigate insurance bureaus, require the filing of rate schedules and other information, and examine rating bureaus periodically. It also prohibits unfair discrimination in fixing or charging fire insurance rates between risks of essentially the same hazards and protection. Furthermore, it details procedures for deviations from bureau rates and prohibits certain contracts related to placing insurance.
classification.reasoning: The statute deals with the regulation of fire insurance rates and prohibits unfair discrimination between risks. There is no mention of race or any indication that it was intended to enforce racial segregation or discrimination. The term 'discrimination' in this context refers to differential treatment of insurance risks based on their hazard level and protection, not racial discrimination. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

It mandates that owners keep buildings safe from fire loss, prevent the public or employees from entering unsafe structures, and implement adequate fire protection measures. The State Fire Marshal is given jurisdiction to enforce these laws and can conduct fire prevention educational campaigns.
classification.reasoning: The statute concerns fire safety regulations for buildings and the powers of the State Fire Marshal. There is no mention of race, nor any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is 'codes' as it appears to be part of a compiled statute collection (Kentucky Statutes, 1918 edition).

classification.title: Kentucky Statutes, 1918, Section 762f-17
classification.summary: This statute grants the State Fire Marshal the authority to prescribe safety methods for buildings, including setting standards for construction, maintenance, and the adoption of protective equipment. It also allows the Fire Marshal to issue general or special orders to ensure buildings are safe from fire loss, with provisions for hearings and public notice of general orders.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text details the powers and responsibilities of the State Fire Marshal concerning building safety and fire prevention. It outlines procedures for issuing orders, setting standards, and conducting hearings. There is no mention of race, nor any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

It mandates that they must file a contract or bond with the Banking Commissioner, agree to service of process through the Commissioner, and provide a written instrument allowing summons to be issued against them from any county in the state. It mandates the disclosure of financial assets, liabilities, stock details, loan terms, and other business information to the Banking Commissioner. Additionally, it requires a deposit of $100,000 in cash or bonds, or a surety bond, to ensure the corporation's financial obligations to Kentucky citizens are met. Failure to comply can result in license revocation.
classification.reasoning: The statute concerns the regulation and financial oversight of foreign corporations operating within Kentucky. It details reporting requirements, financial deposits, and surety bonds to protect the state and its citizens from financial misconduct by these entities. There is no mention of race, segregation, or any discriminatory practices based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: CORPORATIONS - PRIVATE. Banking Commissioner
classification.summary: This statute outlines the requirements for foreign corporations, associations, or societies to do business in Kentucky. It details the process of filing contracts, bonds, and written instruments with the Banking Commissioner, who acts as an agent for service of process. The Commissioner has the authority to issue, revoke, or require new licenses and bonds based on the corporation's compliance with the law and the soundness of its financial condition. Deposits made with the Commissioner are held as security for claims by Kentucky residents.

There is no mention of race, and the regulations apply universally to all foreign entities seeking to operate within the state. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. classification.title: CORPORATIONS - PRIVATE. Banking Commissioner
classification.summary: This statute outlines the requirements for foreign corporations, associations, or societies to do business in Kentucky. It mandates that they must appoint the Banking Commissioner as their agent for service of process, file a contract or bond satisfactory to the Commissioner, and agree to accept summons through the Commissioner. The Commissioner has the power to revoke licenses if these requirements are not met, or if the corporation is found to be conducting business unlawfully, unsoundly, or refuses examination. Deposits made with the Commissioner are held as security for claims of Kentucky residents.
classification.reasoning: The statute concerns the regulation of foreign corporations operating within Kentucky, specifically focusing on their licensing, service of process, and financial security. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly target or discriminate against any racial group. The regulations apply universally to all foreign corporations seeking to do business in the state. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.summary: These sections of the Kentucky Statutes from 1918 outline regulations for foreign corporations, associations, and societies transacting business in the state. They detail requirements for agents to procure certificates, examinations by the Banking Commissioner, and annual financial reports. Specifically, Section 876d mandates a report on assessments, dues, fines, and fees collected from shareholders or stockholders residing in the state, and a tax based on these collections minus amounts loaned back to residents. The sections focus on financial oversight and regulatory compliance for these entities.

It covers aspects like agent certification, banking commissioner oversight, and financial reporting requirements. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly target or discriminate against any racial group. The focus is purely on financial and corporate regulation. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

267 § 10190-1COURTS OF JUSTICE .
SUBDIVISION IVa .
Interpretersin Certain Courts .*
*The Act compiled in thissubdivisionwas Chapter 72a, Section 2223a, of the1915
edition. It was originallySection 1038a of the 1903 and 1909 editions. In the 1915
editionit was entitled, "Interpreter in court with seven judges," but it is suggested
that this designation is too restrictiveas the Act applies to any county now having
or in the future attaining a population of 75,000 and constitutinga separate judicial
district. It was originallyan Act of March 19 , 1894, с. 106,p . 323, entitled"An Act
to authorize the appointment of officialinterpretersin circuitcourts trying criminalcasesin countiescontainingcontaininga populapopulationof seventy-fivethousand or over." At that
time it applied to JeffersonCounty alone, where the circuitcourt was by the Consti-
tution composed of four judges. It was originallycompiled as Sections 1045-1049,
inclusive, of the 1894 and 1899 editionsof the Kentucky Statutes.
By an Act of March 21 , 1902 , с. 55 , p . 113 , the Jefferson Circuit Court was reor-
ganized by providing for six judges and by an Act of the same date, March 21, 1902,
c. 64 , p . 139 , Sections 15-19, inclusive, the said Act of March 19, 1894, was copied
verbatim, except that the district"having fiveor more judges" was substitutedfor
" county containing a population of 75,000 ." This latter Act has become obsolete by
the JeffersonCircuitCourt having been increased to seven judges by an Act of March
15,1912,с. 109, p. 307, governed by an Act of March 18, 1912, с. 118, p . 404, Sections
15-19 of which are identical in terms with the Act of March 21 , 1902 , с. 64 .
By an Act of March 11, 1902, с. 12, p . 37, said Act of March 19, 1894, was , in
effect, repealed. The titleto this Act was , "An Act to amend an Act , entitled, 'An
Act to authorize the appointment of officialinterpreterin circuitcourt trying crim-
inal cases in counties containing a population of seventy-five thousand or over,'
approved March 19, 1894, and to regulate the appointment of officialinterpretersin
circuit courts in such counties hereafter ." Although the whole of the Act of 1894 so
proposed to be amended by reference to its titleis not set forth in the body of the
new Act as itwould appear when amended , as required by Section 51 of the Constitu-
tion as construed in the case of Board of Penitentiary Commissioners v. Spencer,159
Ky . 255,166 S. W. 1017,yet thispart of the titlemay be ignored as surplusage (Bow-
man v . Hamlett , 159 Ky . 184, 166 S. W. 1008 ), and that part of the title, "to regu-
latehereafter," etc., would seem to be sufficientto support the Act and to repeal all
former laws on that subject .
Preceding the enacting clauseof said Act of March 11, 1902, there was a preamble
reading as follows: "Whereas , by an Act entitled'An Act to authorize the appoint-
ment of officialinterpretersin circuitcourt trying criminal cases in counties contain-
ing a population of seventy-five thousand or over,' approved March nineteenth,
eighteen hundred and ninety-four, an officialinterpreterhas been in existencein said
court since the passage of such Act , and whereas a necessity exists that an official

It specifies labeling requirements, including the name and address of the seller, purity percentages, foreign seed content, and germination percentages. It also defines noxious weed seeds and bulbs and sets limits on their presence in seeds sold for agricultural purposes. The statute details how tests for purity and viability should be conducted, who is responsible for them, and the fees associated with tests for non-residents. It also mandates marking for garden and flower seed packets.

It specifies that a conviction cannot be based solely on the testimony of a single witness and requires corroborating circumstances. The statute explicitly states that the general reputation of the accused as a bribe-taker or evidence of past bribery acts are not sufficient corroboration, unless the accused has put their character in issue. Similar provisions are detailed for receiving a bribe to vote.

classification.title: ELECTIONS. § 1596a - 8a
classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1918 pertains to election procedures, specifically addressing the sufficiency of pleadings in contested elections, the eligibility of candidates, the signing and timing of election certificates, the transfer of ballot boxes, the recounting of ballots, the filing of answers and amended petitions, the extension of time for filing transcripts, and the admissibility of ballots as evidence. It also clarifies that certain provisions do not apply to school trustee elections and addresses vacancies in that office. A related section (§ 1596a-3) details the appointment, qualifications, terms, and removal of election officers, and the process for submitting lists of party members for these positions. Another section (§ 1596a-6, repealed and replaced by § 1596a-8a) dealt with canvassing boards for districts spanning multiple counties. The new § 1596a-8a outlines the certification of primary and general election returns for multi-county districts to the Secretary of State and the issuance of certificates by the State Board.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text discusses various aspects of election law in Kentucky, including procedures for contested elections, the role of election officers, and the handling of ballots. While it touches upon the election of school trustees and county superintendents, there is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. The focus is entirely on the administrative and legal processes of elections. Therefore, it is classified as 'no' for Jim Crow, with a high confidence score, and the category is 'voting'. The document type is 'codes' as it appears to be part of a compiled statute book. No human review is needed.

classification.title: Kentucky Statutes, 1918, Chapter 1938a - Game and Fish Laws
classification.summary: This statute outlines regulations concerning the sale, possession, and transportation of various game birds and animals in Kentucky. It specifies unlawful practices related to wild turkeys, pheasants, quail, grouse, doves, prairie chickens, woodcock, deer, and elk. Exceptions are made for transporting hunters with lawfully killed game, and for game raised in captivity or purchased for propagation with proper permits. The statute also grants concurrent jurisdiction to county, justice, and circuit courts for trying offenses and assessing fines, and prohibits trapping game, song, or insectivorous birds. It also sets bag limits for quail and bobwhite.

It also includes provisions for penalties, such as fines and confinement, and the declaration of dogs used in illegal hunting as public nuisances. Several sections are noted as repealed or suspended by later acts.

It outlines penalties for violations, such as fines and jail time, and addresses the issue of dogs used in illegal hunting. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. Therefore, this statute is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is classified as 'codes' because it is presented as part of the 'Kentucky Statutes' which are compiled legal codes.

classification.title: Kentucky Statutes, 1918, Section 1954b-11: Fur-bearing Animals
classification.summary: This statute, enacted in 1916 and codified in 1918, regulates the trapping, shooting, and killing of specific fur-bearing animals (beaver, mink, raccoon, fox, otter, opossum, skunk) in Kentucky. It establishes closed seasons for these animals, with exceptions for raccoons, opossums, skunks, and minks which can be taken by dog or gun during a portion of the closed season. It also allows for the killing of these animals if they are found to be damaging property. Violations are classified as misdemeanors with fines and potential jail time. The statute also includes provisions regarding the prima facie evidence of illegal trapping and possession of animals or their hides.

classification.title: GAMING. Contracts in consideration of, void.
classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1918, specifically § 1955, addresses contracts made in consideration of gaming. It states that such contracts are void. A case note (Holzbo v. Bakrow) clarifies that if the maker of a note induces a purchaser by assuring its validity, they cannot later claim invalidity based on this section. Another section, § 1957, discusses the chancellor's ability to grant relief against a winner in a game, including the right to discover the names of interested parties and the amounts lost.

CHAPTER 74 .

ARTICLE I.
Grand and Petit Jurors - How Obtained .
§ 2247. Jurorsmay be drawn from wheel during court- when by-
standers may be selected.
§ 2247. It is error to direct the sum-
moning of bystanders to supply vacancies
in a jury when the number of vacancies
does not exceed three . L. & N. R. R. Co.
and Curt Jones v. Owens ; same v . Parsons ,
164 Ky . 557 , 175 S. W. 1039 .
The selection of a jury in contravention
of this section is ground for a new trial if
proper exceptions are saved . L. & N. R. R.
Co. c. King , 161 Ky . 324 , 170 S. W. 938 .
Where , during a term of court and prior
to the calling of a case, five jurors have
been excused , and others were selected from
by -standers to take their places on the regu-
lar panel , and when the case was called five
more jurors were required, it was error to
fillthe jury from by -standers, and such error
was not cured by the fact that after per-
emptory challenge only three of those who
were so called remained on the jury . Louis-
ville & N. R. Co. v. King , 161 Ky . 324, 170
S. W. 938 .
If it becomes necessary to summon more
than three jurors to fillvacancies on the
regular panel in order to try a civil ac-
tion, such vacancies must be filledby draw-
ing from the wheel . Louisville & N. R. Co.
v . King , 161 Ky . 324, 170 S. W. 938 .
Where vacancies in the regular panel oc-
curred during a term of court, the court
may in its discretion fillsuch vacancies by
either drawing names from the wheel, or
by directing the sheriff to summon by-
standers to the number of three, and jurors
thus selected may become members of the
regular panel . Louisville & N. R. Co. v .
King , 161 Ky . 324, 170 5. W. 938 .
Where a jury has not been selected in ac-
cordance with the provisions of this sec-
tion, it is ground for a new trial, on the
proper objections, unless the irregularity
has been waived . Louisville & N. R. Co. v .
King , 161 Ky . 324, 170 S. W. 938 .
The purpose of thissectionisto dispense
with professionaljurors, and a verdictby a
jury summoned in substantialdisregard of
the provisions of this section will be set
aside. Louisville& N. R. Co. v. Owens ,164
Ky . 557 , 175 S. W. 1039 .
Where seven bystanders were summoned
at the same time to serve on the jury , it
was held reversible error to overrule a chal-
lenge to the panel . Imperial Jellico Coal
Co. v .Bryant , 168 Ky . 385, 182 S. W. 205 .
Under thissection, it is improper for the
court, where there is a shortage of jurors,
to summon twenty bystanders . Winchester
v. Watson , 169 Ky . 215, 183 S. W. 483 .
Cross reference : See Gregory's Ky . Crim . Law , Sec . 1034 .

§ 2248. Twelve personsconstitute- qualifications- indictment,when

son shallbe qualifiedto serveas a grand juryman unlesshe be a citizen
and a housekeeperofthecountyinwhich he may be calledto serve,and

schools), no surveyor of a highway, tavern-keeper, vender of ardent
spiritsby license,or person who is under indictment,or who has been
convictedof a felonyand not pardoned,shallbe competentto serve as
a grand juror; but the fact that a person not qualifiedor competent
served on a grand jury,shallnot be cause for settingaside indictments
found by such grand jury . (May 22, 1893, с. 210, p. 948, sec. 12, as
amended March — ,1918,с.166,р .672.)

The remaining amount is to be assessed against benefited lands based on classification and ratio. It does not contain any language or provisions that suggest racial discrimination or segregation. The focus is entirely on land assessment and taxation for public works. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: Kentucky Statutes § 2380 (34) - Drainage Bonds
classification.summary: This statute outlines the process for issuing drainage bonds. It details how unpaid assessments for drainage projects can be divided into annual installments, with interest, and how bonds can be issued to anticipate the collection of these assessments. The bonds mature in series corresponding to the installments and bear interest. It also includes provisions for validating past proceedings related to drainage assessments and cost statements.
classification.reasoning: The statute discusses the issuance and payment of drainage bonds, including the process of dividing unpaid assessments into installments and the validation of past drainage proceedings. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial discrimination. The statute appears to be purely administrative and financial in nature, related to public infrastructure projects. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

It also specifies that trials in the circuit court shall be de novo, but no new issues can be raised that were not presented in the county court. The statute also mentions that persons notified to answer and show cause why a report of the board of viewers should not be confirmed are subject to these appeal procedures.

It specifies timelines, required documentation, and procedural rules for these appeals. There is no mention of race, nor any indication of differential treatment based on race. The statute appears to be a procedural civil law governing the judicial system. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

It details the requirements for the petition, including land description, signatures, bond execution, and the appointment of a board of viewers. The board of viewers consists of two resident freeholders and one civil and drainage engineer, with specific qualifications to ensure impartiality.
classification.reasoning: The statute describes the legal procedures for creating drainage, levee, or reclamation districts. It focuses on the administrative and legal requirements for such projects, including petition content, bond amounts, and the qualifications of appointed officials (board of viewers). There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial discrimination. The qualifications for the board of viewers are based on residency, age, property ownership within the proposed district, and kinship to petitioners, none of which are race-based criteria. Therefore, this statute is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.summary: This statute outlines responsibilities for repairs to drainage improvements. It states that if a landowner's actions, negligence, or livestock cause damage or obstruction to a drainage improvement, the landowner is responsible for making the repairs at their own expense. Failure to do so within thirty days of notification by the board of drainage commissioners constitutes a misdemeanor. The board can remove obstructions and charge the cost, plus interest, to the landowner, creating a lien on the land.
classification.reasoning: The statute addresses the maintenance and repair of drainage improvements and the liabilities of landowners for damage caused by their actions or livestock. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial discrimination. The statute appears to be a civil or administrative regulation concerning land use and infrastructure. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the process for establishing a levee. It requires a petition signed by at least five landowners, detailing the necessity, route, and affected landowners. A bond must be posted to cover expenses and damages. The county judge then appoints three commissioners to assess damages and compensation for land acquisition. These commissioners, along with a surveyor, will survey the levee route, determine land requirements, identify owners and tenants, and assess compensation. They will also report on the public benefit of the levee. If the levee is not deemed of public benefit, the commissioners will report this finding.

fifteenyears after an oral partition vested
in each the titleto the part allotted him .

The grantee in a void deed purporting
to convey land does not by paying taxes
acquire title in the absence of actual pos-
session of the land . Kypedal Coal & Lum-
ber Co. v. Millard, 165 Ky . 432, 177 S. W.

The mere grazing or pasturing of live
stock on uninclosed land is not adverse
possession of same . Ky . Coal Lands Co. v .

§ 2505. Adverse possession of a tract of
twelve hundred acres for fifteen years was
held to be also adverse possession as to
four smaller tracts embraced within it
against joint owners . Mounts v . Mounts ,
155 Ky . 363 , 159 S. W. 818 .
The possession of certain land in this
case was not adverse to the claim of the
father of the person in possession. Rice
v . Blair, 161 Ky . 280 , 170 S. W. 657 .
There cannot be two constructive pos-
sessions of the same land at the same time .
Frazier v . Ison, 161 Ky . 379 , 170 S. W. 977 .
Limitation does not run against a lien
holder while in possession of the property .
Possession which is not continuous for fif-
teen years will not confer title. A holding
under and with one rightfully in possession
was not adverse possessionagainst others
having interestsupon the facts of this case.

W. 951
VI . SURETIES
2548 .
STOLEN PROPERTY .
A married woman has a right to sue for
possessionof her land without joiningher
husband . Limitation begins to run against
her from the time the ction accrues and
runs during coverture, but extends until
three years after she becomes discovert.
Big Sandy Co. v . Ramey , 162 Ky . 236 , 172
S. W. 508 .
Possession taken under a deed of a mar-
ried woman in which her husband did not
join is adverse to her. A cause of action
to recover the land accrued as soon as
such possessionwas taken. Big Sandy Co.
v . Ramey , 162 Ky . 236, 172 S. W. 508 .
Where possession is taken under an oral
partition and is held adversely for fifteen
years the possession vests title in per-
son so holding. Henderson v. Clark, 163
Ky . 192, 173 S. W. 367 .
A certain instruction as to the kind of
adverse possession which will give title to
land was improper . Terry v . Loudermilk ,
158 Ky . 353, 164 Ky . 959 .
A person occupying enclosed land does
not hold it adversely beyond the true line
if he only claims up to the true line wher-
ever it may be . Turner v . Morgan , 158
Ky . 511 , 165 S. W. 684.
The possession of one who entered on
land under a deed regularly put to record
was held to be adverse possession; and from
the time of the entry limitation ran in his
favor. Meyers v.Forstman, 6 Ky .Opinions
94 .

tered has no force except to show the ex

classification.summary: This statute outlines various legal actions that must be commenced within one year of the cause of action accruing. These include actions for personal injury (to plaintiff, wife, child, ward, apprentice, or servant), injury to cattle or stock by railroads or corporations, malicious prosecution, conspiracy, arrest, seduction, criminal conversation, breach of promise of marriage, libel or slander, actions against physicians or surgeons for negligence or malpractice, and actions for the escape of a prisoner on civil process. classification.title: Receiving or accepting liquor carried into prohibited territory for profit unlawful; each package a separate offense.
classification.summary: This statute makes it unlawful for any person or corporation to receive or accept intoxicating liquor from a common carrier or other person who transported it into a territory where sales are prohibited, if the transportation was for compensation, hire, or profit. Each package received or accepted in such territory constitutes a separate offense. Exceptions are made for shipments in transit to other states or to areas where sales are lawful, for licensed druggists for medicinal or scientific purposes, and for wine delivered to a church officer for sacramental purposes.
classification.reasoning: The statute addresses the prohibition of intoxicating liquors in specific territories within Kentucky. It focuses on the logistics of receiving and transporting alcohol into these 'dry' areas, rather than on racial segregation or discrimination. There is no mention of race, and the regulations apply universally to anyone violating the prohibition laws. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is 'codes' as it is presented as a section within the Kentucky Statutes (1918).

classification.title: MEDICINE AND SURGERY. § 2618a-1 - § 2618a-5
classification.summary: This statute, enacted in 1916 and codified in 1918, addresses the unethical practice of fee-splitting between medical professionals without the patient's consent. It defines 'selling the patient' as a physician referring a patient to another for treatment and receiving payment without the patient's knowledge. Conversely, 'buying the patient' is defined as a physician knowingly receiving such a referred patient and paying for the referral. Penalties include fines and, for a second offense by a physician or surgeon, forfeiture of their license. The statute also clarifies that the 'seller' is not an accomplice of the 'buyer' and can be compelled to testify, though their testimony cannot be used against them.
classification.reasoning: The statute deals with professional conduct and ethics within the medical field, specifically concerning fee-splitting arrangements. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that would implicitly or explicitly create racial segregation or discrimination. The penalties and regulations apply universally to all physicians and surgeons regardless of race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is classified as 'criminal_laws' because it defines offenses and penalties, including misdemeanors and license forfeiture.

The provisions governing the National Guard will apply to the organization, enlistment, equipment, armament, discipline, government, regulation, pay, service, trials, discharge, and mustering out of the Kentucky State Guard, with certain exceptions.

It also forbids owners, proprietors, managers, or employees of public accommodations (hotels, opera houses, skating rinks, etc.) from denying admission or discriminating against members of these military organizations based on their uniform. Exceptions are made for theatrical professionals and cadets pursuing military instruction. Violations are punishable by jail time or a fine.

classification.title: Kentucky Statutes, 1918, § 2711a -135 to § 2711a -138
classification.summary: These sections of the Kentucky Statutes from 1918 outline the duties and penalties for civil officers in relation to the Kentucky National Guard, and regulate the assembly and drilling of armed groups. Specifically, § 2711a-135 mandates civil officers to assist the National Guard upon request, with penalties for failure to comply. § 2711a-136 prohibits unauthorized military companies or armed organizations from drilling or parading without the Governor's license, with exceptions for benevolent/social organizations wearing swords and students in military science programs. Penalties are prescribed for violations. § 2711a-137 details the duty of Commonwealth and county attorneys to provide legal advice and assistance to National Guard commanding officers. § 2711a-138 requires approval from regimental commanders or higher authority for parades or voluntary service by military companies under arms or in uniform. § 2711a-139 addresses medical care for disabled National Guard members.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute sections (§ 2711a-135 to § 2711a-138) deal with the organization, duties, and regulation of the Kentucky National Guard and other armed groups. There is no explicit or implicit mention of race, segregation, or any discriminatory practices targeting specific racial groups. The regulations pertain to military conduct and the enforcement of military law, not to civil rights or social segregation. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the duties, salary, and appointment process for the Chief Inspector of Mines and three additional Assistant Inspectors of Mines in Kentucky. It details their qualifications, responsibilities related to mine safety and inspection, and administrative provisions such as office location and rent allowances. The law was enacted in response to the rapid increase in the number of coal mines.
classification.reasoning: The statute pertains to the regulation and inspection of mines for safety purposes. It details the administrative structure and qualifications for mine inspectors. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly or explicitly discriminate based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is inferred as 'session_laws' due to the citation format (e.g., 'March 26, 1918, c.25, p.76, sec.1').

classification.title: Kentucky Statutes, 1918, Section 2722
classification.summary: This statute outlines the duties and responsibilities of assistant mine inspectors in Kentucky. It details their appointment, bonding requirements, salary, and expenses. Their duties include inspecting coal mines, enforcing mining laws, training miners in rescue methods, responding to mine emergencies, and reopening sealed mines. The statute also describes the chief inspector's role in supervising inspections, collecting statistics, maintaining records, and dividing the state into inspection districts, assigning assistant inspectors to these districts.
classification.reasoning: The statute text provided details the administrative and operational aspects of mine inspection in Kentucky, including the roles and responsibilities of inspectors and the chief inspector. There is no mention of race, segregation, or any differential treatment based on race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is inferred as 'codes' because it refers to 'Kentucky Statutes' and specific section numbers, suggesting a compilation of laws rather than individual session acts.

classification.title: Mines and Mining - Reports and Statistics
classification.summary: This statute outlines the reporting requirements for coal mine operators to the Chief Inspector of Mines in Kentucky. It details the information to be included in annual and monthly reports, such as coal production, consumption, and mining methods. The statute emphasizes the confidentiality of individual operational data, which is to be published only in aggregate form. It also specifies penalties for failing to provide the required information.
classification.reasoning: The statute pertains to the reporting and statistical requirements for coal mine operations in Kentucky. It details the types of information that mine operators must submit to the Chief Inspector, including production, consumption, and mining methods. The statute also addresses the confidentiality of this data and penalties for non-compliance. There is no mention of race, and the regulations appear to apply universally to all mine operators regardless of race. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: Kentucky Statutes - Ventilation and Drainage, Shot Firers, Discretionary Powers of Assistant Inspectors, and Appointment of Assistant Inspector
classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1918 covers various aspects of mine safety and regulation. It details the duties of mine superintendents and foremen, the rights of miners injured due to lack of ventilation, the responsibilities of shot firers, and the discretionary powers and appointment of assistant mine inspectors. classification.summary: This statute requires chauffeurs and demonstrators operating motor vehicles in Kentucky to wear a badge issued by the board of examiners. The badge must display the license number and the word "Ky.". Failure to display the badge results in a fine and license cancellation. Lost badges can be replaced for a fee. Wearing a fictitious badge or a badge after a license has expired or been cancelled incurs a fine and prevents future licensing. Conviction for drunkenness while operating a vehicle leads to license forfeiture. It is unlawful to employ an unlicensed chauffeur or demonstrator, with a fine for employers. Temporary licenses may be issued.

It details the requirements for ordinances, public notification, petition filing in circuit court, defense by resident voters, and the criteria for court judgment based on the majority of resident voters' remonstrance and potential injury to property owners. The process involves court proceedings, and if the judgment is adverse, further attempts are prohibited for two years. Costs follow the judgment, and appeals are permitted.
classification.reasoning: The statute describes the procedural requirements for municipal boundary changes in Kentucky. It focuses on the legal steps, public notification, and judicial review of annexation or detachment of territory. There is no mention of race, and the criteria for approval or denial are based on the majority of resident voters' wishes and potential injury to property owners, not on racial considerations. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.summary: This statute outlines procedures for municipal corporations of the fourth class in Kentucky regarding street, alley, sidewalk, and public way improvements. It details how assessments for improvements are to be handled, emphasizing that funds from one improvement cannot be diverted to another. It also allows city councils to decide by ordinance whether the city will pay a portion of the improvement costs, with such provisions needing to be uniform and subject to decennial changes. The text also includes case law interpretations related to the validity of assessments for street improvements, guttering, and curbing, and the liability of property owners and cities for such work.
classification.reasoning: The statute pertains to municipal improvements and financial procedures for cities of the fourth class. It discusses the allocation of funds for street and sidewalk improvements and the process for assessing costs to property owners. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly suggest racial discrimination. The case law cited also deals with the legality of assessments and contract modifications for public works, not racial segregation or discrimination. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: Kentucky Statutes, Section 3577
classification.summary: This statute outlines the process for issuing and managing municipal bonds for public improvements. It details the requirements for bond signatures, negotiability, exemption from defenses, and sale conditions. It also specifies how premiums and penalties are to be used, the exclusive source of payment for the bonds, and the redemption process for bonds, including notice requirements. Furthermore, it states that after bond issuance, no suit can be filed to enjoin or resist the collection of assessments or taxes in anticipation of which the bonds were issued, and the validity of such assessments and taxes cannot be questioned, with property owners being estopped from assailing their effectiveness or validity. The statute also grants bond owners liens on the assessments and taxes, with the power to enforce collection through foreclosure if bonds or coupons are not paid.

Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

It references several Kentucky court cases to support its points.

classification.title: NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS
classification.summary: This section of the Kentucky Statutes from 1918, specifically § 3720b-103, details the rules for providing notice of dishonor for negotiable instruments when the parties involved reside in the same place. It clarifies that notice given the day after dishonor is sufficient and modifies previous rules regarding the timing of mailed notices, making them valid if deposited in the post office in time to reach the recipient in the usual course on the second day. It also applies to situations where the recipient's post office is in the same place as the dishonor, even if they don't live there.
classification.reasoning: The provided statute text pertains to the legal procedures for handling negotiable instruments, specifically concerning the notification of dishonor when parties reside in the same locality. There is no mention of race, segregation, or any differential treatment based on race. The statute focuses solely on commercial law and procedural aspects of banking and finance. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is inferred as 'codes' because it refers to numbered sections within a larger compilation of statutes (e.g., § 3720b-103).

§ 3720b -104 732KENTUCKY STATUTES .
§ 3720b-104. Noticewhen theyliveindifferentplaces.
§ 3720b,subsec. 104. Notice depositedin
the mail on the day or day after the day
of dishonor was sufficient . Hickman v .
Ryan , 5 Litt. 24; Stiversv. Prentice, 3 В.
Mon. 461 ; Mitcherson v . Grays , 4 B. Mon.
399; McClane v.Fitch,4 B. Mon. 600.
See also Miller's Ky . Neg .Inst., p . 133 .
Cross reference: See Miller'sKy .Nego .Inst.L.,p .133.
§ 3720b-105. Noticemay be sentthrough mail.
§ 3720b , subsec. 105. While the holder
is only requiredunder the above sectionto
mail the notice duly addressed , yet both
these facts are essential . McGowan v . Bank
of Kentucky , 5 Litt. 271; Taylor v.Bank of
Illinois, 7 T. B. Mon. 576 .
Cross reference: See Miller'sKy .Nego .Inst.L.,p . 134.
§ 3720b -106 . Notice when mailed .
§ 3720b , subsec . 106. Since under section
105 the sender is deemed to have given no-
tice when he has mailed the same properly
addressed , it would seem that in order to
avail himself of this presumption of law,
he must comply strictly with this section.
Hence he must prove that the proper notice
was deposited in a postoffice, or branch
postoffice, or a letter box under the con-
trol of the Postoffice Department .
Cross reference: See Miller'sKy .Nego .Inst.L.,p .135.
§ 3720b -107. Notice of dishonor to antecedent parties.
§ 3720b , subsec. 107. See Triplett V.
Hunt , 3 Dana 126 ; Smith v . Roach , 7 B.
Mon. 17 .
In the case of Williams v . Paintsville
Nat . Bank , 143 Ky . 781, 137 S. W. 535,
the meaning of the word " antecedent" was
called in question. The defendant , one of
several joint endorsers, was the only one
notifiedof the non -payment of the note . He
contended that he could not notify the
others because they were joint endorsers
with him and none of them were antecedent
to him . In response to this the court said :
" Antecedent parties within the meaning of
section107 are those antecdentin liability,
and to whom the person giving the notice
has a right to look for reimbursement; for
by section 90 any party to the instrument
may give the notice 'who upon taking
it up would have the right to reimburse-
ment from the party to whom the notice is
given.' As to his part of the debt, a joint
endorser may be looked to for reimburse-
ment by his co-endorser who receives notice
of dishonor from the holder. As to his part
of the debt he is an antecedent party ; for
to this extent it is, as between them , his
debt . The operation of section 107 is not
confined to those who are antecedent in
liabilityas to the whole of the debt ; but it
applies to all who are antecedent as to any
part of it. The endorsers know their rela-
tion to each other better than the holder,
and the purpose of the act is to provide a
uniform rule which the holder may follow
in all cases as the rule was applied in the
case of successive endorsers at common
law ."
Cross reference: See Miller'sKy .Nego .Inst.L.,p . 135.
§ 3720b -108. Notice sent to address given .
§ 3720b , subsec. 108. Subsection 1 was
the law . Bondurant v . Everett , 1 Met . 658 .
The place where a billwas dated was pre-
sumed prima facie to be the residence of
the drawer and payee. Page v. Prentice, 5
B. Mon. 7 .
Where the person to be notified is a
transient person , a notice sent to his most
usual place of resort is good . McClain v .
Waters , 9 Dana 55 .
Where the notice is actually received
within the legal time , it matters not how
or where it was sent. McClain v. Waters,
9 Dana 55 ; Moreland v . Citizens' Savings
Bank , 97 Ky . 211, 30 S. W. 637, 17 K. L.
R. 88; Monarch v. Farmers ' etc.,Bank , 105
Ky . 430 , 49 S. W. 317 , 20 K. L. R. 1351 .
Cross reference : See Miller's Ky .Nego . Inst . L. , p . 137 .
§ 3720b-109. Noticemay be waived.
§ 3720b , subsec 109. Before the passage
of this act the law was that, where an en-
dorser or drawer had been released by rea-
son of not having been given the proper
notice, a mere promise made thereafter to
pay the instrument was without considera-
tion and uninforcible . Lawrence v . Ral-

261; Bank of Tennessee v.Smith, 9 B. Mon.
609; Bank of United Statesv. Leathers, 10
B. Mon. 64 ; Landrum v . Towbridge , 2 Met .
281; Sebree Deposit Bank v. Moreland, 96
Ky . 150 , 28 S. W. 153, 16 K. L. R. 404. And

§ 3720b, subsec. 109. Notice of dishonor
may be expresslyor impliedlywaived be-
fore or after time of notice. Doherty v .
FirstNat . Bank of Louisville, 170 Ky . 810,
186 S. W. 937 .
Cross reference : See Miller's Ky . Nego . Inst . L., p . 138 .
§ 3720b -110 . Notice waived in instrument .
§ 3720b , subsec . 110. A waiver embodied
in the face of the instrument is binding on
allparties. Bryant v. Merchants ' Bank , 8
Bush 43; Smith v. Lockridge, 8 Bush 423;
Swope v. Boone County Deposit Bank , 101
S. W. 334, 31 K. L. R. 48; Owensboro Sav-
ingsBank & Trust Co., etc.v. Haynes , 143
Ky . 534, 136 S. W. 1004; Atkinson v. Skid-
more , 152 Ky . 413 , 153 S. W. 456 .
See alsoMiller'sKy . Neg . Inst., p. 140.
§ 3720b -112. When notice of dishonor dispensed with .
§ 3720b , subsec. 112. See Lawrence v .
Ralston , 3 Bibb 104. As to duties of a
notary public where he does not know ad-
dress of party to be notified, see note to
section 118 .
Cross reference : See Miller's Ky . Nego . Inst . L. , p . 141 .
§ 3720b -113. Notice, when delay of excused .
§ 3720b , subsec. 113. See Lawrence v .
Ralston , 3 Bibb 102. The existence of the
Civil War furnished a good excuse , where
one of the parties was in the Confederate
and the other in the Federal lines, Berry v .
Southern Bank of Kentucky , 2 Duv . 382.But when communication was regularly
opened , the excuse for further delay ceased .
Morgan v . Bank of Louisville, 4 Bush 82 .
The facts, that the holder of a draft ac-
cepted from the acceptor a check on a bank
in a distant city in payment of the draft
and then cancelled the draft and delivered
it to the acceptor and the check was dis-
honored , do not show that the delay in giv-
ing notice to an endorser was caused by
circumstances beyond the control of the
holder . Nor does the fact that the endorser
was not damaged by the delay affect the
question. Young v.Exchange Bank ,152 Ky .
293 , 153 S. W. 444 .
Cross reference : See Miller's Ky .Nego . Inst . L., p . 141.
§ 3720b -114. When noticenot required to be given to drawer .
§ 3720b , subsec. 114. The maker of a
note payable to his own order and endorsed
by him , is not entitled to notice. Pace v .
Welmending , 12 Bush 142. The same is
true of an accommodation maker . Marion
Nat . Bank v. Phillips, 35 S. W. 910, 18 Κ .
L. R. 159 .
If the drawer had no funds in the hands
of the drawee and if he had no right to
expect the drawer to honor the bill he was
not entitled to notice. Humphries v . Bick-
nell, 2 Litt.296 ; Clarke v . Castleman , 1 J. J.
Mar. 70 ; Taylor v . Bank of Illinois, 7 T. B.
Mon. 581 ; Barbaroux v. Waters , 3 Met . 304.
Cross reference : See Miller's Ky .Nego . Inst . L. , p . 142 .
§ 3720b-115. When noticeto endorser not required.
§ 3720b , subsec. 115. The fact that the
endorser is not injured by reason of failure
to receive notice in due time does not dis-
pense with such notice. Young v. Exchange
Bank , 152 Ky . 293 , 153 S. W. 444 .
Where the proceeds of a note were paid
by the payee to the maker , the fact that the
money was lent at the request of the en-
dorser and on his credit, does not show
that the note was made for the endorser's
accommodation . The person accommodated
is the one who gets the money . First Nat .
Bank v .Bickel , 143 Ky . 754, 137 S. W. 790 ;
Grayson County Bank v . Elbert , 143 Ky .
750, 137 S. W. 792. See also Mechanics ' &
Farmers ' Savings Bank v . Katterjohn , 137
Ky . 427 , 125 S. W. 1071, and First Nat .
Bank v.Bickel, 154 Ky . 11, 156 S. W. 856.
Where a note was executed to cover a debt
from the maker to the payee ,the fact that it
was discounted by a bank as a favor to the
payee , does not bring the case within the
rule laid down by subsection 3, for the note
was not made for the payee's acommoda-
tion but to evidence a debt from the maker
to him . Brown v . Crofton , 76 S. W. 372 , 25
K. L. R. 753 .
Cross reference : See Miller's Ky . Nego . Inst . L. , p . 144.

classification.title: Notice of Dishonor
classification.summary: These sections of the Kentucky Statutes (1918) detail the requirements for providing notice of dishonor for negotiable instruments. They cover when notice is sufficient, how it can be sent (through mail), when it is deemed given, and to whom it should be sent, including antecedent parties. The interpretation of 'antecedent parties' is clarified to include those antecedent in liability for any part of the debt, not just the whole. It also addresses notice to transient persons and the effect of actual receipt within legal time, regardless of how or where it was sent. Finally, it touches upon the waiver of notice.

classification.title: Negotiable Instruments - Material Alteration
classification.summary: This statute, specifically section 3720b, subsection 125, defines what constitutes a 'material alteration' in a negotiable instrument. It states that an alteration is material if it changes the legal effect of the obligation. It also clarifies that certain changes, like adding 'or order' to a promissory note, are now considered material, distinguishing negotiable from non-negotiable instruments. Tearing off a negotiable note from a larger document is not considered a material alteration if the holder is in due course.

Protest .
§ 3720b -152. When protest required.
§ 3720b , subsec. 152. Section 483 of Ken-
tucky Statutes is repealed by this act. Wil-
liams v. PaintsvilleNat . Bank , 143 Ky .
781, 137 S. W. 535; Southern Nat .Bank v .
Schimpler, 159 Ky . 373, 167 S. W. 148.

§ 3720b -153. What protest must show .
§ 3720b , subsec. 153. When the bill pro-
tested is shown to be the bill sued on , the
mere fact, that the protest showed that the
last endorsee was the holder, does not de-
prive the real holder of the benefit of the
protest. Thus where the last endorsee was
a holdermerely for collection,the realown-
er may strikeout the endorsement to such
holder, and sue on the billas owner and
use the protestas evidence in his behalf.
Bank of Tennessee v . Smith , 9 B. Mon. 612 .

§ 3720b-154. By whom protestmade .
§ 3720b , subsec . 154. The fact that the
notary who protested the bill, was also the
cashier of the holder bank , did not dis-
qualify him as notary . Moreland v . Citi-
zens' Savings Bank , 97 Ky . 211, 30 S. W.
637, 17 K. L. R. 88. See also Miller'sKy .
Neg . Inst., p. 191.

§ 3720b , subsec. 155. In Smith v . Roach ,

the 19th, 1842. John D. Campbell , Not .
Pub . N. Y.," was competent evidence as to
the fact of presentment for acceptance and
dishonor, that where a presentmentwas
made by a notary and the bill was dishon-
ored and protestedthisfact couldbe proven
by any other evidence in their power .

§ 3720b-161. Acceptance for honor .
§ 3720b , subsec. 161. It will be noticed
that there can be no acceptance for honor
until after protest.

an acceptance for honor ; and only one on
payment for honor (Gazzam v. Armstrong,
3 Dana 554 ) which will be referred to under
the next article. [Ed .]

TitleIII.— Promissory Notes and Checks .
ARTICLE I.
§ 3720b -184. Negotiable promissory note.
§ 3720b , subsec. 184. Although it was
held in Piner v. Clary, 17 B. Mon. 645, that
a certificateof depositby reason of itsen-
dorsement became a bill of exchange , yet
under this act, we think , it would be a
promissory note. See Krebs v. Blatz, 134
Ky . 505, 121 S. W. 436, and authorities
cited .
While a surety, on a promissory note , is
liable only as surety as against a payee
with knowledge of the fact that he is a
surety, Weller v. Ralston, 89 S. W. 698, 28
K. L. R. 572 , yet under this act he is only
a maker and therefore not entitled to pre-
sentment,demand or notice,Frittsv. Kirch-
dorfer, 136 Ky . 643 , 124 S. W. 882. Nor
can an endorser for accommodation be
treated as a surety. First Nat . Bank v .
Bickel , 143 Ky . 754, 137 S. W. 790 ; Gray-
son County Bank v . Elbert , 143 Ky . 750,
137 S. W. 792 .
The note sued on in Mechanics & Farm-
ers' Savings Bank v. Katterjohn, 137 Ky .
427 , 125 S. W. 1071 , possessed all the re-
quirementsof negotiabilityrequiredby this
act. See on this point Wettlaufer v . Bax-
ter, 137 Ky . 362 , 125 S. W. 1071 , where it
was held that a note not payable to order
or to bearer was not negotiable.
Cross reference: See Miller'sKy .Nego .Inst.L.,p .207.
§ 3720b -185 . A check .
§ 3720b, subsec. 185. While it is a gen-
eral rule that a bank must know the signa-
tures of its depositors, and having paid a
forged check to a holder in due course can-
not recover back the money (Deposit Bank
of Georgetown v .Fayette Nat .Bank , 90 Ky .
10, 13 S. W. 339, 11 K. L. R. 803 ), yet where
the paying bank failed to have the holder
identified and paid the forged check upon
a forged endorsement , and thereafter the
check was paid by the bank upon which it
was drawn , it was held that the money
could be recovered by it from the paying
bank , because first, of the negligence of
the paying bank in not requiring identifica-
tion and , second, because the paying bank
warranted the forged endorsement . Farm-
ers' Nat . Bank v . Farmers ' & Traders '
Bank , 159 Ky . 141, 166 S. W. 986 .
§ 3720b , subsec. 185. In view of this
subsectionand subsecs. 132, 143, 144, 189,
relatingto checks and billsof exchange, a
bank was held not liable where the drawee
of a check withdrew allhis depositbefore
presentation of the check . Ewing v . Citi-
zens' Nat . Bank , 162 Ky . 551, 172 S. W.
955 .

§ 3720b -186. When drawer discharged from payment .
§ 3720b , subsec . 186. It was held that
where one acquired title to a check two
days after it was drawn , he took it before
it was overdue. Asbury v. Taube , 151 Ky .
142 , 151 S. W. 372 .
Cross reference : See Miller's Ky .Nego . Inst . L. , p . 220 .
§ 3720b -187 . Certifiedcheck equivalent to acceptance.
§ 3720b , subsec. 187. The certificationof
a check makes the bank , so certifying, an
insurer of the check ; and a bank which
has received such a certified check may
permit the one who deposits it to withdraw
the proceeds after it has received notice of
its protest and dishonor , and still be
holder for value . First Nat . Bank v . Bank
of Ravenswood , 141 Ky . 671 , 133 S. W. 581 .

classification.summary: These statutes, § 3720b-188 and § 3720b-189, outline the conditions under which a bank is liable for a check. Certification of a check by the holder releases the drawer and endorsers, as certification is equivalent to withdrawing the money and redepositing it to the holder's credit. A bank is only liable once it has accepted or certified a check; prior to that, it is not liable for refusal to pay, even if the drawer has insufficient funds. The text also references related subsections concerning checks and bills of exchange and cites relevant court cases.

classification.title: POOLS - TRUSTS - CONSPIRACIES
classification.summary: This statute prohibits unfair discrimination in pricing of commodities by businesses operating in Kentucky. It defines unfair discrimination as selling a commodity at a lower rate in one section, community, or city than in another, after accounting for quality and transportation costs, with the intent to destroy a competitor's business. Corporations found guilty of this can have their right to do business in the state forfeited. Violators are guilty of a misdemeanor and subject to fines. Prosecutions can be initiated in Franklin Circuit Court or any circuit court where the offense occurred. The statute also grants circuit courts jurisdiction to prevent and restrain illegal combinations, pools, trusts, confederations, conspiracies, promises, or understandings.

It includes penalties for the county attorney failing to notify the State Tax Commission of appeals.
classification.reasoning: The statute deals with the administrative process of tax assessment appeals. It does not contain any language, explicit or implicit, that suggests racial discrimination or segregation. The procedures described are general and apply to all taxpayers. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: REVENUE AND TAXATION - TRANSIENT MERCHANTS
classification.summary: This statute outlines regulations and penalties for transient merchants in Kentucky. It specifies that certain sales, such as farm produce and fire insurance loss adjustments, are exempt. It also details how license fees are to be collected and paid into the state treasury. Furthermore, it establishes penalties for violations and outlines the process for enforcement, including the duty of state agents and county officials. A key provision is that licenses will not be granted to individuals who have previously engaged in business without a license within the preceding six months, or who refuse to answer questions under oath about such past violations. A penalty of an additional sum equal to twenty percent of the regular license tax is imposed for such past offenses.
classification.reasoning: The statute concerns the regulation and licensing of transient merchants, including penalties for violations and requirements for obtaining a license. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly target or discriminate against any racial group. The regulations appear to be purely economic and administrative in nature, applying to all individuals conducting business as transient merchants. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.

classification.title: ROADS - PUBLIC
classification.summary: This statute outlines regulations for public road maintenance and employment. It specifies that employees can be hired and discharged at pleasure by the fiscal court or county judge. It also details compensation for road workers, mandating prevailing wages for manual labor (between $1 and $3 per day) and higher rates for skilled labor, foremen, and assistant engineers (up to $5 per day). A day's work is defined as at least eight hours of actual labor. Additionally, it mandates that landowners bordering public highways must clear brush, weeds, shrubs, and overhanging branches, and keep hedges trimmed to a maximum height of five feet, with penalties for non-compliance. The county road engineer is responsible for publishing notices of these duties.
classification.reasoning: The statute concerns the management and maintenance of public roads, including employment and compensation for road workers, and the responsibilities of landowners to clear vegetation along highways. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that implicitly target or discriminate against any racial group. The regulations apply universally to all individuals and landowners involved in public road maintenance and adjacent property upkeep. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law. The document type is 'codes' as it appears to be part of a compiled statute collection (indicated by section numbers like § 4342a-3 and references to previous acts and court cases). The category is 'labor' due to the detailed provisions on employment and wages for road workers.

classification.title: Eligibility and Election of County Superintendent in Counties with Separate School Systems
classification.summary: This statute outlines the eligibility requirements for the office of county superintendent in counties that have a system of public schools separate and distinct from the common schools of the county, specifically in counties embracing a city of the first or second class. It mandates that such a superintendent must be a resident of the county outside of the city or town. It also lists other county officials and teachers who are ineligible to hold the office of county superintendent. The statute further details the election process, term of office, and bond requirements for county superintendents. A key provision states that in counties with separate school systems in cities of the first or second class, the county superintendent must reside outside such cities and be elected by voters residing outside those cities.
classification.reasoning: The statute mandates separate school systems in counties with cities of the first or second class. The provision that the county superintendent must reside in the portion of the county *outside* of such city or cities and be elected by voters residing *out of* such city or cities, in the context of separate school systems, strongly implies a racial segregation component. Historically, separate school systems in the Jim Crow era were established along racial lines, and this residency and voting restriction for the superintendent in such a context would have served to maintain that segregation. While race is not explicitly mentioned, the structure of the law points to an implicit racial purpose within the broader Jim Crow framework of separate but unequal facilities.

classification.summary: This statute outlines the requirements for obtaining teacher certificates in Kentucky, including an oath to prevent cheating on examinations. It details the content of the oath, the process for distributing and preserving it, and penalties for non-compliance by educational officials. It also mentions a previous version of the section being repealed and replaced by a new act.
classification.reasoning: The statute focuses on the administrative and ethical aspects of teacher certification, specifically addressing the integrity of examinations. There is no mention of race, nor are there any provisions that would implicitly create racial segregation or discrimination within the education system. The language is neutral and applies to all applicants for teacher certificates. Therefore, it is not a Jim Crow law.
